bio.en: Graham Weaver teaches a top-rated course at Stanford's Graduate School of Business and is the founder and CEO of Alpine Investors, one of the world's top-performing private equity firms; he helps people get off 'autopilot' and figure out what to do with their lives.
bio.zh: Graham Weaver 在斯坦福商学院开设一门高评分课程，同时是 Alpine Investors（全球表现最顶尖的私募股权基金之一）的创始人兼 CEO；他帮助人们摆脱“自动驾驶模式”，想清楚自己这辈子该做什么。

summary.en: Graham shares practical frameworks for finding your path, including the 'genie' thought experiment (what would you wish for if any wholehearted pursuit were guaranteed to succeed?) and the 'nine lives' exercise. He argues that life is suffering, so you may as well choose something meaningful, and that everything you want lies on the other side of 'worse first'—the hard early days you must push through. The conversation also covers when to actually quit, and how to escape the autopilot mode most people live in. His advice comes from someone actively doing the work, not just teaching it.
summary.zh: Graham 分享了找到人生方向的实用框架，包括“神灯精灵”思维实验（如果任何全身心的追求都 guaranteed 成功，你会许什么愿？）和“九条命”练习。他主张人生本就充满苦难，所以不如选择有意义的事；你想要的一切都在“先苦后甜”的另一侧——你必须熬过那些艰难的开头。对话还涵盖了究竟何时该放弃，以及如何摆脱大多数人都在过的“自动驾驶”模式。他的建议来自一个真正在做事、而非只教书的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.zh: 整个讨论与你大力倡导的理念息息相关——即摆脱生活的自动驾驶模式。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver

turns.zh: 我们处于无意识状态，可能甚至不明白自己为何要做正在做的事，甚至不清楚自己在做什么。比如，我起床、锻炼、开车上班、应对堵车、通勤、回复邮件、下班路上继续堵车、匆忙吃晚餐。这不是一个有意为之的一天。我从未问过自己：“我的人生该走向何方？这个世界对我而言什么才是重要的？”

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yeah, that is accurate. About half of all the times I meet with students, that's the question they ask. It's really funny too, because sometimes they'll come with a PowerPoint presentation and a two-by-two matrix and an expected value and all that. But really they're asking the question of, "Hey, what should I do with my life," which is, by the way, a great question.
turns.zh: 是的，这很准确。大约一半的学生咨询时都会问这个问题。其实挺有趣的，因为有时他们会带着PPT演示、二维矩阵、期望值之类的东西来。但实际上他们问的还是"嘿，我的人生该怎么过"，而这恰恰是个很棒的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Why do you think that's the case? That's not what I would imagine someone at an MBA school in a business class asking for advice on.
turns.zh: 你觉得为什么会这样？这不是我想象中商学院MBA课程的学生会寻求建议的内容。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: My typical meeting with a student will say, the student will start to tell me about these two or three different career or job alternatives that they have, A, B and C. Let's just use two, A and B. And then they go through and they start talking about A, and they tell me all the pros and the cons of A, and they go through it. And then they go through B, and they start telling me all those things. And I start asking some questions. (00:06:56): And after about five or 10 minutes into that, I can tell that their heart and their soul and their energy is really for B. That's really what they want, but they're talking themselves out of B, and they're going to talk themselves into A. So what I try to do is, A, first, I try to let them realize that their real energy is for B, just let them feel that and understand that. And then secondly, I try to figure out, what are the limiting beliefs they have? What are the fears? What are the obstacles? What are the voices in their head? What are all the societal pressures that are keeping them from doing B? And then we try to deconstruct those and get them to go do B. So that's the process.
turns.zh: 我和学生们的典型会面是，他们会开始列举自己可能选择的两到三个职业或工作方向，比如A、B和C。暂且用A和B来举例。他们会逐一讨论A的优缺点，然后再讨论B。我会提出一些问题。在五到十分钟的讨论后，我能感觉到他们的热情和精力都倾注在B上。这才是他们真正想要的，但他们在说服自己选择A。我的做法是，首先，让他们意识到自己真正的热情在B，帮助他们感受到并理解这一点。其次，我会分析他们有哪些限制性信念、恐惧、障碍，以及脑海中的声音，还有哪些社会压力在阻碍他们选择B。然后我们一起拆解这些障碍，鼓励他们去选择B。这就是整个过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of a student going ... just this actual conversation you had with someone?
turns.zh: 有没有学生真正经历过这样的对话的例子？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Absolutely. So there's a great example of a student of mine was from Brazil. And he came in and his prior job prior to business school was he worked in consulting. And that was more or less what he wanted to do. And then at some point I asked the students, "Okay, imagine you knew you were going to be successful and you were going to have a dream. And whatever you dreamed was going to come true, what would you dream for?" And he wanted to start a nonprofit in his home country of Brazil to help students have more access to education. That was what came up for him. (00:08:27): And over the course of our class, we just chipped away at all the fears and limiting beliefs of why he shouldn't or couldn't do that. And by the end, that's what he did. And so that's a real life example. And there's all kinds of other examples, but that second one of going and starting a charity, it's not on the beaten path. It's not what probably your parents are thinking you should do. There's probably 100 reasons not to do it. You probably don't know exactly how to start, and so it's intimidating. But if you start with this idea, "Hey, five years out, 10 years out, I know I'm going to be successful," and work backwards from that, you're going to come up with a better answer.
turns.zh:
没错。有一个很棒的例子，我的一位学生来自巴西。他来上课之前，在商学院之前的工作是做咨询，这也是他当时想做的。但后来我问学生们：“好吧，如果你知道自己一定会成功，并且能实现任何梦想，你会许什么愿呢？”他说想在巴西创办一家非营利组织，帮助当地学生获得更多教育机会。这就是他的梦想。

（00:08:27）在我们的课程中，我们不断消除他心中的恐惧和自我设限的信念。到课程结束时，他真的实现了这个目标。这就是一个真实的案例。还有很多类似的例子，但创办慈善机构这条路并不寻常，可能也不是你父母希望你走的路径。肯定有上百个反对的理由，你甚至不知道如何起步，所以这很让人却步。但如果你从这个想法出发：“五年后，十年后，我知道自己一定会成功。”然后倒推回去，你就能找到更好的答案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is a framework that you call the genie methodology or the genie framework, this question that you just asked that we should spend more time on, which is ... I guess, you tell the story of the genie and how to think about this [inaudible 00:09:20].
turns.zh: 这就是你称之为"精灵方法"或"精灵框架"的思维模式，你刚刚提到的那个问题值得我们深入探讨，我猜你讲的是精灵的故事，以及如何思考这个问题[00:09:20未录音]。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Well, when I was 13 years old, I used to listen to these motivational tapes, mowing lawns. And I'm pretty sure it was Brian Tracy had this exercise. And I've adapted it, so I'll use my exercise now. So I say basically imagine that you're walking home from work and you see this bright, shiny object. You walk over and you realize it's a magic lamp. And you rub the lamp and this genie comes out and the genie says, "Hey, I haven't been in this bottle for 10,000 years yet, so I'm not fully formed. So I can't give you three wishes. But what I can do is I can give you one wish. And the wish I can give you is whatever you throw yourself into with your whole life and your career, it's going to turn out great. It's going to work out great. It's probably going to take longer than you think. It's going to be harder than you think, but you're going to be really happy you did and it's going to work out beyond your wildest imagination." If that were true and you had that genie blessing you with that wish, what would you wish for? (00:10:19): And then the students come up with an answer that's really close to their heart. It's a thing they would do, absent the fear of failure. And then the second part of the exercise is basically that's what you should go do. You should be spending your life in pursuit of your genie goal. Maybe you can't start that tomorrow; you have financial obligations, maybe there's some experience you need. But at some point in this one life we get, you want to get yourself on that path of that journey. And that's the exercise that I go through with the students.
turns.zh: 嗯，我13岁的时候会在修剪草坪时听励志磁带。我很确定布莱恩·特雷西（Brian Tracy）有过一个练习。我对此进行了改进，现在我会用自己的练习方法。基本上，我会让你想象自己下班回家，看到一个明亮闪亮的物件。你走过去，发现是一盏魔法灯。你擦擦灯，精灵出现后说：“嘿，我在瓶子里待了一万年，还没完全成形，所以不能给你三个愿望。但我可以给你一个愿望。无论你全身心投入到生活和事业中的任何事情，都一定会成功。过程可能比你想象的更漫长，挑战也更大，但你一定会为自己的选择感到欣喜，而且结果会超出你的想象。”如果这是真的，精灵用这个愿望祝福你，你会许什么愿呢？（00:10:19）然后学生们会给出一个贴近他们内心的答案。这是他们即使没有失败恐惧也会去做的事。接下来练习的第二部分基本上就是：你应该去做这件事。你应该用一生去追寻你的精灵目标。也许你明天无法开始，但你有经济负担，或许还需要积累经验。但在我们有限的生命里，你应该踏上这条旅程。这就是我和学生们一起进行的练习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a simple idea, that I can totally see how it could be so powerful. And I love the way it's framed as not like it'll guarantee you'll be successful. It's instead, I'll guarantee you'll be happy.
turns.zh: 这是一个非常简单的想法，我完全能理解它为何如此强大。最重要的是，它不是保证你一定成功，而是保证你一定快乐。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver

This charity to start education for underprivileged kids in Brazil, that takes its own form over the course of a decade. And it will almost certainly turn out differently than you think. So it's more that you'll be really happy you went and started that journey, and it will go great. It'll probably go differently and take longer than you think though.
turns.zh: 你会为自己选择了这条道路而感到欣慰。之所以这么说，是因为天赋型目标往往是那些少有人走的路。所以你甚至不确定目标究竟是什么。比如，在巴西为弱势儿童创办教育项目，这个事业在十年间逐渐成形。结果很可能与你的预期大相径庭。因此，更重要的是你会为踏上这段旅程而心怀感激，整个过程也会顺风顺水。不过，旅程可能会比你想象的更曲折、耗时更久。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are some other examples of genie goals folks have followed that are kind of non-traditional and they've ended up being happy about it?
turns.zh: 还有哪些天赋型目标的例子呢？人们追随的这些目标往往非传统，却最终收获了满满幸福。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Mine was buying companies in my dorm room at business school. I have a student who's starting an amusement park in Texas. That's a pretty crazy example. Many students who are leaving their job and doing startups. A lot of students who going in the nonprofit world. So really just lots of examples. It's as variant as the number of students I have. And that's the magic of it, because you have inside of you some really unique dream that you maybe haven't even shared. And the goal is that that's your uniqueness, and that's what you should be bringing into this world.
turns.zh: 我自己就是在商学院宿舍里收购公司。还有个学生要在德州开主题公园，这真是个疯狂的例子。许多学生辞职创业，很多人投身非营利领域。这样的例子数不胜数，数量之多正如我学生们的多样性。这就是其神奇之处，因为你内心深处藏着独特的梦想，可能甚至从未与人分享过。关键在于，这种独特性正是你的天赋所在，也是你应该带入这个世界的财富。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This whole exercise connects to something that you're a big advocate of, this idea of getting out of autopilot mode in your life. And the way I think about it is people ... and I'm going to ask you to describe it, but just it's almost like you're driving and you've never turned off the cruise control in your car, and you don't realize it. Talk about this idea that most of us are in autopilot and why it's so important to realize that and get out of it.
turns.zh: 整个练习与你大力倡导的理念息息相关——摆脱生活中的自动驾驶模式。我想请你描述一下这个概念，就好像你在开车时从未关闭过定速巡航，却浑然不觉。谈谈大多数人处于自动驾驶状态的原因，以及为何清醒意识到这一点并摆脱这种状态如此重要。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: You start off and you're unconscious, and you're kind of going through the motions. And you may not even realize why you're doing what you're doing or even realize what you're doing. So for example, a typical person gets up, they have whatever their morning routine ... I'll use myself. I get up out, work out, take a shower, drive into work, fight traffic, commute. I'm late. I get in, I'm late to a meeting, I'm kind of rushed meeting; meeting, meeting. Okay, quick break for lunch. Maybe I return some emails; a few more meetings, a couple of Zoom calls. Fight traffic on the way home, rush through dinner, get back on email. Go to bed. Okay, that's my day. And that's a busy day. I felt like I did a lot. I'm exhausted, but it's unconscious. (00:13:45): It's not a day that is intentional. It's not a day where I've said, "Where do I want to be going with my life? What's important to me in this world? What are my values? What 10 years from now will I wish I was starting to embark on?" Adding that level of intentionality and then working backwards from that is really the magic of getting to that 10 years from now and looking back without regret and getting to a later point in your life and feeling like you're doing the thing you're put on the earth to do as opposed to just going through the motions.
turns.zh: 你起初浑浑噩噩，只是机械地重复日常流程。甚至可能不知道自己为何要做现在做的事，也不清楚自己在做什么。比如，典型的一天：起床，完成晨间例行事务（拿我自己举例）——锻炼、洗澡、开车上班、堵车、开会……开会、开会。午餐时间快速休息，回复邮件、再开几次会、打几个Zoom电话、回家堵车、匆忙吃晚餐、继续回复邮件。然后上床睡觉。这就是我的一天。忙碌却毫无意识。这不是有意为之的一天。我从未问过自己：“我的人生目标是什么？这个世界对我重要的是什么？我的价值观是什么？十年后我希望开始做什么？” 加入这种自觉意识，再从此处倒推，才是通向十年后回首时无悔人生的魔法之路，也是通向人生后半段、做自己命中注定要做之事的秘诀，而非仅仅是机械地重复日常。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So the question then here is, how do you get out of that autopilot mode? Because first of all, no one really realizes this is the case. And I'll tell a quick story. We're going to different preschools and daycares for our son. He's a year and a half oldish. And we went to this Montessori school, and the teacher's like, "I'm going to be very clear: what we're doing here is informing your child's subconscious. That's what they're learning here. And that's a huge responsibility. We put a lot of love into that idea, but it's very important you understand that's what we do at the school." And I never thought of it that way.
turns.zh: 那么，问题来了，如何摆脱这种自动驾驶模式呢？首先，人们通常并未意识到这种情况。我来讲个小故事。我们带儿子去了几家不同的学前班和日托所。他现在一岁半左右。我们去了一家蒙台梭利学校，老师说：“我要明确一点：我们在这里做的是塑造孩子潜意识的工作。这才是他们在这里学习的核心内容。这是一项重大的责任。我们投入了大量心血，但你们必须清楚，这就是我们学校的教育理念。” 我从未以这种方式思考过这个问题。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: That's amazing that they said that. So you just opened up another part of this, which is depending on what research you read, somewhere between 95% and 98% of our thoughts are subconscious. And those get programmed in somehow, some way. A big part of that, by the way, is media, our friends, our parents, our boss, our coworkers, what we think we're supposed to do, social media: "This is cool, buy this Ferrari," all these different things. And then you're just operating out of that. And so the idea of being intentional is create space, get out of that, get out of the fog of war, make some space. We'll probably get to this in a little bit, but I do it with an executive coach, and really ask deep questions, make space, ask questions, create the intention that you want in each of the areas of your life. And then start having your calendar reflect that intention.
turns.zh: 他们这么说真是令人惊讶。这让我们延伸出另一个观点——根据一些研究，人类95%到98%的想法都是潜意识的。而这些想法在某种程度上被编程进我们的思维。其中很重要的一部分来自媒体、朋友、父母、老板、同事，以及我们认为应该做的事，比如社交媒体上的那些诱惑：“买这辆法拉利吧！”等等。然后我们就被这些想法所左右。因此，有意识地生活意味着创造空间，跳出这种思维定式，拨开迷雾，留出空白。我们稍后会详细探讨这个话题，但我自己会通过执行力教练来做到这一点，深入自问，创造空间，提出问题，明确自己在生活各方面的意图。然后让日程安排来映射这些意图。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so this genie exercise is one approach, is just ask yourself this question. Can you say it again just for folks so they don't miss it, what's the question you should ask yourself?
turns.zh: 那么，这个“精灵练习”就是一个方法，就是问自己这个问题。如果你知道自己不会失败，你会做什么？这才是最重要的问题。如果你想听更多，我可以继续。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: I mean, the biggest question I think with respect to your career is, within reason, what would you do if you knew you wouldn't fail? That's the biggest question. I'll give you a few more if you want.
turns.zh: 是的，请继续。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, please.
turns.zh: 好的，请。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Different questions trigger different things with people that could be helpful, trigger in a good way. So here's a few more. If you didn't have to make money, what would you do? And that'll answer what you enjoy. Naval Ravikant has a great question, which is, what's play for you that is work for other people? So for you, Lenny, that might be a podcast. That might be play for you; that's really fun. You're always going to do better at that. You're going to spend more time, you're going to enjoy it more. That's a good one. (00:17:00): Another one is, what's the thing you really want to do? But you're just too embarrassed to say it? And my answer to this question was that I wanted to be a motivational speaker like Tony Robbins. And I was super embarrassed to say that, but that actually works into a lot of my life at this point. Another question, who are some people that you admire and want to be more like, and what do they do? Where do you find those people? What are some things you want to learn and how do you want to grow over the next five, 10 years? So I know a lot of your listeners are working in tech. So five, 10 years from now, you're amazing, you're best in the world at X. What's X? And how do you start to work toward becoming great at X? So there's just a few more other questions you could throw in to help you figure out some things you're excited about.
turns.zh:
不同的问题会激发人们不同的潜能，以积极的方式触发灵感。所以这里还有几个问题。如果你不需要赚钱，你会做什么？这能揭示你的兴趣所在。纳瓦尔·拉维坎特提出了一个很棒的问题：对别人来说是工作的事，对你来说是什么？对莱尼来说，这可能就是播客。这对你来说就是玩乐，很有趣。你在播客上会表现得更出色。你会投入更多时间，也会更享受这个过程。这是个好问题。
（00:17:00）：另一个问题是，你有没有想做却又不好意思说的事？我的答案是，我想成为像托尼·罗宾斯那样的励志演说家。我当时特别不好意思说这个，但现在这确实融入了我的生活。还有一个问题：你欣赏并想效仿的榜样是谁？他们做了什么？你在哪里能找到这些人？未来五年、十年，你想在某个领域成为世界顶尖高手，那个领域是什么？你要如何朝着这个目标努力？对于很多科技从业者来说，五年、十年后，你会成为行业巨星，世界顶尖高手。在那个领域，你要如何开始成长？所以还有很多其他问题可以抛出，帮助你发现自己热爱的事物。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned this idea of limiting beliefs. And I think a lot of people listening to this are probably having these beliefs right now of, "Okay, but I have a family to support. Am I going to go start a charity in Brazil? That's absurd. It sounds easy, but I can't actually change my life this radically." Can you just share something to help people get past that in some way?
turns.zh: 你提到了限制性信念这个概念。我想，听这期播客的很多人可能现在都有这样的信念，比如：“好吧，但我得养家糊口。我要去巴西创办慈善机构吗？这太荒谬了。听起来容易，但我根本无法彻底改变自己的生活。” 你能否给出一些建议，帮助人们克服这些心理障碍？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Sure. The first thing I would say about limiting beliefs is they're the most powerful and the most dangerous when you don't even know what they are. So when they're in the recesses of your subconscious mind, that is 95% of your thoughts, that's when the limiting beliefs are the most dangerous. (00:18:32): So a simple example might just be like I have a limiting belief that I'm not funny. That's in my subconscious and I don't even realize I have it. So I avoid things where I'm trying to be funny or tell jokes. I mean, that's a silly example. But let's use your career now and come up with some maybe deeper ones. Let's use that charity example, the Brazilian charity, "I'm going to start a Brazilian charity." What are the limiting beliefs? Well, oh my gosh, there's a million. "I don't know how to start. I don't know how I would pay for myself. I have business school debt. I don't really know what I'm even talking about. I don't even have a plan for it. How would I get funding?" Those are all these things that are flooding your mind. (00:19:15): So the first exercise is just write all that down. Just get it down on paper, and then two things will happen. One is when you get it down on paper, it will almost immediately strip that limiting belief of a lot of its power and a lot of its scariness. Because now it's just something like, for example, "How would I fund this?" So the second thing that is that a lot of that scariness becomes just a to-do item. In the recesses of your subconscious, that is a very scary, limiting belief that will actually keep you from doing the thing you love. Once it's on paper, now it's just a to-do item that you can actually deal with with your conscious mind, just like you do anything else. So, "How would I fund this," just becomes a plan, like, "I need to design a plan where I'd get funding for this charity." And then that just is a problem like any other problem. It's not this nebulous, scary fear. It's just literally a to-do item. (00:20:14): So the first part of limiting beliefs, write them down, understand what they are, look at them in the cold day of light on paper, and then translate them into things that are just obstacles to be overcome. And by the way, if you're listening to this podcast, you've overcome millions of obstacles in your life, and these are no different once they're down on paper.
turns.zh: 当然。关于限制性信念，我首先想说的是，当你甚至不知道它们是什么的时候，它们最强大也最危险。所以当它们深藏在潜意识里，占据你95%的思维时，才是最危险的。（00:18:32）举个简单的例子，我有个限制性信念，觉得自己不幽默。这在潜意识里，我自己都没意识到。所以我会回避任何需要展现幽默感或讲笑话的场合。这是个挺傻的例子。但现在我们来谈谈职业发展，用巴西慈善机构的例子来说：“我要在巴西创办慈善机构。” 那有哪些限制性信念呢？天哪，太多了。“我不知道怎么开始。不知道如何自负盈亏。背负着商学院的债务。根本不知道自己在说什么。甚至没有计划。怎么才能获得资金？” 这些念头在你脑海中涌现。（00:19:15）第一个练习就是把这些都写下来。写在纸上，然后会发生两件事。一是写下来后，限制性信念的力量和恐惧感会迅速削弱。因为现在它只是个问题，比如“如何获得资金？” 第二，恐惧感会变成待办事项。在潜意识里，这是一个可怕的限制性信念，会阻止你追逐热爱的事业。一旦写下来，就成了待办事项，用理性思维就能应对。例如，“如何获得资金？” 就成了计划：“我需要设计一个融资方案。” 然后这就成了普通问题，不再是模糊的恐惧。（00:20:14）限制性信念的处理步骤：写下来，理解其本质，用理性思维转化为可克服的障碍。顺便说一句，如果你正在听这期播客，你已经克服了生活中的无数障碍，写下来后这些问题也不例外。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Are you actually doing these exercises with your students? They're taking a class about growing their enterprise and then it's like, "Okay, let's analyze what you want to do with your life"? Is that how this class goes?
turns.zh: 你真的在给学生做这些练习吗？他们上的是创业课程，然后就是：“好，我们来分析你的人生目标。” 课程是这样进行的吗？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: That's a really good question. So I'll give you a little bit of background. So I was a case guest at Stanford Business School while I was buying companies in my dorm room. And it was talking about all the things that went wrong. And so it's kind of a really fun case. And I did that for 12 years. And I started to realize that was my most energetic day of the year. And so long story short, I started teaching a class full time. So I did that for four years. And I was teaching the Xs and Os of being a CEO, basically: hiring, firing, having hard conversations, managing a board, fundraising, selling, all the things you would imagine that a young CEO would need to know. (00:21:20): After about four years, I started to realize that was great, except that no one went and did it. So the class is on entrepreneurship, and they learned how to be an entrepreneur. There was only one problem: they didn't actually become entrepreneurs. So then I said, "Well, wait a sec. I have to readjust my class a little bit, and I have to spend some time on the stuff we've just been talking about: finding out what your dream is, your limiting beliefs, starting to map out goals toward your actual entrepreneurship dream or whatever your genie goal is." (00:21:53): So the way I say it is the university allows me to teach the class because I teach them entrepreneurial tricks, tactics, tools that will help them become a great CEO. But the real reason I teach is because I'm trying to help people really go find the thing that they're excited about and get into the life path of doing that thing. So I do both, but I do the second one kind of ... maybe that's not the headline of the course, although I think that's probably why people like the course so much.
turns.zh:
这真是个好问题。我先给你们讲讲背景吧。我在斯坦福商学院做案例分析的时候，正好在宿舍里收购公司。当时我们讨论了所有失败的案例。这其实是个挺有趣的案例。我做了12年这件事，然后意识到那是我一年中最充满活力的一天。长话短说，我开始全职授课，教了四年。主要讲CEO的方方面面：招聘、解雇、艰难谈话、管理董事会、融资、销售等等——都是年轻CEO需要掌握的技能。（00:21:20）四年后，我发现虽然课程很棒，但没人能真正去实践。所以我改了创业课，让学生学习如何创业。但问题是，他们并没有真正成为创业者。所以我调整了课程，花时间教他们如何找到梦想、突破自我限制、规划实现创业目标的路径。

（00:21:53）我这么说吧：大学允许我开这门课，是因为我教给他们创业技巧、策略和工具，帮助他们成为优秀的CEO。但我真正教学的目的是帮助人们找到自己热爱的事业，踏上追梦之路。所以我两者都做，但重点在于……虽然这可能不是课程的核心卖点，但我想这正是人们喜欢这门课的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like a Trojan horse element.
turns.zh: 这就像个木马计。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Exactly, yeah. Tony Robbins used to say that people hire him for success, and he has to give them that so that he feels like he earned his money, but what he really delivers them is fulfillment. And it's a little bit like that. People take my class to learn how to be a CEO, but what they really get is hopefully on the path of doing the thing they want to do.
turns.zh: 没错。托尼·罗宾斯曾说，人们雇他是为了成功，但他得先传授成功之道，这样才能觉得自己值回票价。但他真正给予的是满足感。这道理有点相似。人们来上我的课是为了学做CEO，但最终希望能踏上追梦之路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of what you've been talking about, it's almost an assumption that you'll be more successful and happier if you follow your energy, your passion, versus the, "Here's how I'll make a bunch of money. Here's how I'll move up the ladder." Can you speak to that?
turns.zh: 你讲的很多内容都基于一个假设：如果顺从自己的热情和激情，就会更成功、更快乐，而非追求“赚大钱、步步高升”。你能谈谈这个观点吗？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yeah. Gosh, Lenny, it sounds so cliche when you say it like that, that I almost cringe a little bit. Let me try to give it a little bit different framework where it won't sound as ... because cliches are cliches because they're true. But let me try to give you a little bit different framework to think about it. (00:23:29): I think about it as you have sort of your heart or your soul or your internal scorecard, and then you have your head and your mind and the world's external scorecard. And I'll speak from this from experience. So when I graduated from business school, I took the job I was supposed to take. And it was the safe job at the big private equity firm that paid well and looked great on my resume. And I took that job. That was the external scorecard. My head said that. I built an expected value calculation, all that stuff. (00:24:02): The problem was it wasn't my internal scorecard. It had nothing to do with what I actually cared about and wanted to do with my life. And so the way that shows up is just this tension, friction, stress, anxiety, burnout, all those things. And you can will that, you can will yourself through for long periods of time. In fact, if you want, you can will yourself through that your whole life. (00:24:31): But then once I got into the path of the thing that I was excited about, that's when I really felt my energy change dramatically. And I developed almost a superpower in that thing, because I had more energy. I was willing to work longer, I was willing to do it. I've been running my company now for 23 years. I was willing to do it for a longer period of time. I thought about it in the shower. I thought about it when I went on runs. I talked to people. They wanted to join because I was excited. And it was a whole different level of power and life force that I was able to bring to that. (00:25:14): So I'm saying this from experience, that you're going to show up so much differently in the thing that you're excited about, that that alone is going to make your life a lot better. But the great irony is you're going to do so much better in that thing than you are the thing you are, quote, "supposed to do." And I certainly, certainly understand that people have real life constraints on their finances. And I 100% get that. And so a big part of what I do with students is work through those things and say, "Okay, great. Let's talk about this job you're going to take for X years and you're going to pay off your loans or whatever. But during that time, let's get you on the path of the thing you really want to do." So sometime soon in your life, you want to get on that path.
turns.zh: 是啊。你看，莱尼，你这么说听起来太老生常谈了，以至于我都有点听不下去了。让我试着换个角度来讲讲这个问题，这样听起来就不会那么……因为陈词滥调之所以成为陈词滥调，是因为它们说到了真相。但让我试着给你一个不同的框架来思考这个问题。（00:23:29）我把它想象成，你内心深处有自己的理想、灵魂或内在评判标准，然后还有你的头脑和外界的评判标准。让我用亲身经历来举例。当我从商学院毕业时，我接受了本该拒绝的工作。那是一家大型私募股权公司的安稳工作，薪资丰厚，简历上也很光鲜。我接受了这份工作。那是外界的评判标准。我的理智告诉我这么做是对的。我计算过预期价值，考虑了各种因素。（00:24:02）但问题是，这根本不符合我内心的评判标准。这与我真正在乎的、想为生活做的事毫无关联。结果就是产生了巨大的内心冲突、压力、焦虑和倦怠。你可以强迫自己坚持很久。事实上，如果你愿意，你可以用这种方式度过一生。（00:24:31）但当我开始追随自己热爱的事业时，我才真正感受到能量的大爆发。在那件事上，我几乎获得了超能力般的专注力，因为我更有活力。愿意投入更多时间工作，愿意坚持下去。现在我经营公司已经23年了。我愿意为此付出更长时间的努力。我在洗澡时思考，在跑步时构思，与人交流。他们想加入是因为我充满热情。我能为此注入完全不同的生命力和能量。（00:25:14）所以我要告诉你，追随自己热爱的事业会让你焕然一新，仅此一点就能让生活好太多。但最大的讽刺是，你在真正热爱的事业上会比所谓“应该做的事”做得好得多。我完全理解人们在财务上受到现实限制，这点我百分之百感同身受。因此，我与学生的合作重点之一，就是帮助他们克服这些现实问题，说：“好的，很棒。先谈谈你接下来要从事的X年工作，或者还清贷款之类的。但在这期间，让我们先踏上你真正想做的事业之路。”总有一天，你也会踏上这条路。

turns.en: Okay, so the short answer is I don't know, because I don't have full information about how my students do or what their path would have been had they not done it. You excited about something. We just talked about what that is. The decade or more is going to come true more likely if you're excited about it. But also, you have to go in at the beginning with that mindset and the structural ability to stay at it for a long period of time. So the missing ingredient in most of the people that fail is time. (00:28:18): And I'll use myself as an example. I started Alpine. We lost money on our first fund. We started doing well. We got hit by the recession, we started digging out, whatever. But long story short, I was 14 years into running my firm until I could say with confidence we were going to even stay in business, let alone be really successful. But if you take away the time period, then I would've gone down as one of the, quote, "failures," as opposed to, I would say, one of the success stories using this methodology. (00:29:10): So time is the variable. And I think the biggest part of that is it's really, believe it or not, not typically the finance or the structural piece. It's the entrepreneur or the individual's willingness to actually stay with it. And then upstream of that, it's their belief about how long it's supposed to take. And I really hate this about the social media and just media in general, where they try to paint this picture that things are going to happen overnight. And we've invested in 600 businesses. Let's say 550 of those are founder-started businesses where we're the first money. I've never, in one of those examples, seen anyone who did something quickly. They've all been very, very long stories to get to that point.
turns.zh: 好吧，我不知道，因为我没有完整的信息来评估学生们的表现，也不知道如果他们不这么做，人生轨迹会如何。所以这个问题很难回答。但我想说，成功的公式是你对某件事保持热情十年或更久。所以关键点是什么？你得对某件事充满热情。我们刚刚谈到了这一点。十年或更久的时间只有在你对此充满热情的情况下才更有可能实现。但同时，你必须从一开始就带着这种心态，并具备长期坚持的能力。所以大多数失败者的共同缺失因素就是时间。（00:28:18）：以我自己为例。我创办了Alpine。我们第一只基金亏损了。后来情况好转了。但我们遭遇了经济衰退，开始艰难前行，总之历经波折。直到14年后，我才有信心说我们能继续经营下去，更不用说取得真正的成功了。而用外界标准衡量，直到18年后我们才算真正成功。如今23年过去了，我们一直发展得很好。但如果忽略时间维度，我可能会被视为失败者，而不是成功者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me of a quote I read. I don't know if you wrote this or you shared it, this idea that the life is suffering, so choose something worth suffering for.

turns.en: I wrote that, yeah.

turns.en: You wrote that. Talk about that, because it feels like it's exactly what you're describing. It's going to take a long time to figure something out.

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I know those are two non-super optimistic quotes perhaps, but I think they're true. The second one, everything you want is on the other side of worst first, and this is something where I almost can't think of many exceptions to this. Pick anything. You want a better body? Okay, you're going to need to go to the gym. When you go to the gym the first few times, it's going to not be that fun. You're going to set your alarm, you're going to get sore. It's not going to be great. You're going to have to probably make some changes to your diet. That's not going to be fun, at least initially. And so that's one example. (00:32:05): You want to change careers, you're going to have to learn a new career. You're going to have to leave your career. You're going to have to maybe interview for new jobs, or whatever it is. In each case, the first move is negative. The first move is negative to getting in shape. The first move is negative to get out of a bad relationship, to get into a career you want to be in. The reason I think that's important to say is because if I'm optimizing for tomorrow and I just want to have a great day tomorrow, I'm going to stay exactly where I am, because my life will be better tomorrow if I don't make any changes. I don't have to break up with my girlfriend, have a hard conversation, have the tears, be alone, go on dating apps. I don't have to do that if I just stay in it one more day. (00:32:55): So if you realize this and instead ask the question, the version of myself five years from now, what would they wish I was going to do right now? And if you can make decisions from that, and then on top of that, realize it's going to get worse first, then that's why I say everything you want is on the other side of worse first. But if you don't do that, you just end up plateauing. And so many people I see have this happen where they hit a plateau and they never move past it because they're not willing to have that hard day, month, week, year whatever it is.
turns.zh: 是啊，我知道这两句话听起来不太乐观，但我认为它们确实有道理。第二句“你想要的都在更糟的境遇之后”，这个观点几乎无处不在。举个例子：你想拥有更好的身材？好吧，你得去健身房。刚开始去几次，肯定没那么有趣。你得设定闹钟，忍受肌肉酸痛，过程并不愉快。至少一开始你得调整饮食习惯。这肯定不轻松。再比如，你想转行，就得学习新技能，离开现有职位，或许还要面试新工作。在每个转变中，第一步都是消极的。健身的第一步是消极的。摆脱糟糕关系的第一步是消极的。进入理想职业的第一步也是消极的。我觉得强调这一点很重要，因为如果我只为明天优化生活，期待明天能过得开心，那我就会原地踏步，因为不做出改变，明天的生活确实会更好。分手？不用面对艰难对话，不必流泪，不必独自面对约会软件。再坚持一天就行了。（00:32:05）所以如果你意识到这一点，转而问问五年后的自己：现在你希望我做什么？我敢保证五年后的你会说：“无论接下来两个月多痛苦，都要摆脱这段有毒的关系。”如果你能从这个角度做决定，再加上“更糟的境遇之后才有你想要的”这个认知，那么一切都说得通了。否则你就会停滞不前。我见过太多人因为不愿经历艰难时期而停滞不前。

turns.en: Yeah. For people that are listening and be like, "Okay, I'm motivated. I want to do this," other than taking your class, anything you can recommend to just do these sorts of exercises, ask yourself these questions that you've seen work?
turns.zh: 是的。对于正在听节目的听众，如果他们想说：“好吧，我受到了启发，我想这么做”，除了参加你的课程，还有什么建议可以让他们多做这类练习，多问自己这些已经被证明有效的问题？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: I mean, the answer is accountability. How do you keep yourself accountable to living the life you want to live? And the analogy I would use is let's say that your number one goal in life is you've got to get in better shape. You just have to. Let's say you have even medically, you're going to have real health problems if you don't do that. I would say you hire yourself a personal trainer, pay what you need to pay. Okay, maybe you don't have a ton of money, but that's where I'd spend it. That person, A, they're going to hold you accountable to showing up at a certain time, and B, they're going to show you the exercises. They're going to call you if you're not there. You're just increasing the chances of success. Plus you spend some money, you want to get your money out of it. (00:37:40): The equivalent of that in your life is an executive coach. And I figured this out in 2009 in the dark recesses of the recession. I hired my first executive coach. And I was like, "Wow, it's a personal trainer for me for two things." Number one, make space to ask yourself the big questions in life about your career, your relationships, your health, your spirituality, your children. Whatever the big things are in your life, ask the big questions, find out what your intention is. What are you looking for in those areas? And just have, in my case, several hours a week to get clear on those things. Okay, so that's part one. (00:38:25): And then part two is that person can hold you accountable. I have one coach that I can't even have the call with the coach unless I fill out a piece of paper or an online form that says, "Here's what my one year goals are, outcomes I want to have this year are. Here's what I did last week, based on those. Here's what I'm going to do next week toward those. And here's the outcomes I want to have for the call we're about to have." And even if I never had the call, just having to fill that out every single week is incredibly powerful and allows me to hold myself accountable. (00:39:03): So 100%, that's what I'd recommend. Let's back up and say, okay, let's say you can't afford a coach or you're worried about that. And this is the same thing as, let's say you couldn't afford a personal trainer. I would give you the same advice, which is find a very like-minded friend of yours and sit down and do it for each other. So if you're using the workout example, okay, you're going to go on a run Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Fridays with your friend, and they're going to meet you at 7:00 AM at this trail, or 6:00 AM at this trail. That's your accountability. And you're going to be more likely to do it. You don't want to let them down. They're going to beat you up if you don't get there. (00:39:44): Same is true with this. This is how I started. I did this with my roommate in business school. And we would go on a walk for 30 minutes and talk about my dreams and hopes. Then we'd turn around and talk about his. And it was great, because we made room for each other to have those conversations, and we also developed a great friendship. So short of having an actual executive coach, find a really-minded person that could get into this with you, and that would be another thing. But accountability is huge. I'm going to just say one more thing. I'm sorry. I'm going on a little bit long on this.
turns.zh:
我的意思是，关键在于责任感。你如何才能做到对自己负责，过上理想的生活？我打个比方，比如说你人生首要目标是改善健康状况。你必须这么做。假设你因为健康问题不采取行动，后果会很严重。我会建议你聘请私人教练，愿意花多少钱就花多少钱。好吧，也许你没那么多钱，但这笔钱花得值。教练会督促你按时到场，指导你锻炼。若你没出现，他们还会联系你。这能大大提升成功几率。再说钱的问题，你肯定想让这笔钱花得值。

（00:37:40）人生中类似的角色就是高管教练。2009年经济低迷期，我想到了这个点子。我聘请了人生首位高管教练。他就像是私人教练，帮我解决两大问题：一是为事业、人际关系、健康、精神追求等人生重大议题留出思考空间；二是设定目标并追踪进展。比如每周抽出几个小时专注这些问题。

（00:38:25）第二点是教练的责任监督。我的教练要求我每周填写表格，详细列出年度目标、上周行动计划和下周执行方案。即便不通话，每周填表的仪式感也极具约束力，能有效监督自己。

（00:39:03）百分之百推荐这种方式。退一步说，如果你请不起教练或有所顾虑，那就找志同道合的朋友互相监督。比如每周二、三、五晨跑，约定7点或6点集合。这种互助式问责能显著提高执行力。

（00:39:44）我就是这么开始的。商学院时和室友每周散步30分钟，先聊我的梦想，再听他的畅想。这种互助机制不仅增进了友谊，还让彼此的成长得以同步。

turns.en: There's another thing that happens that's kind of magical, which is you activate a different part of your brain when you talk. You actually activate more of your brain when you talk than when you think or write. So thinking activates the least amount of your brain. Writing is a little bit better, but talking activates a whole different region of your brain. So that's the other big benefit of not doing this just on your own, is being able to talk about it with someone.
turns.zh: 还有一件事也很神奇，那就是当你说话时，你会激活大脑的不同区域。与思考或写作相比，谈话时大脑激活的区域更多。因此，思考所激活的大脑区域最少，写作稍好一些，但谈话能激活大脑的完全不同区域。所以，不独自行动的另一个重要好处，就是能与他人交流想法。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that there's a whole spectrum of ways to create accountability for yourself. I love the second coach you've shared, where just filling out that form was basically the biggest benefit.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏为自己设定责任追究机制的多种方式。我特别喜欢你分享的第二位教练的做法，光是填写那份表格本身就是最大的收获。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: I learned this from these audio tapes. When I was in college, I had this green notebook. And I was trying to row crew, and I never row crew before. And I wrote down at the top of the page every single morning, I wrote down, "I am the number one rower in the country." I wasn't. I was a freshman novice, 135 pound Midwesterner, never had been in a boat. But I wrote that down. And then I wrote down three things I was going to do that day to move toward that goal. And I did that every single day that I was in college. And it's just incredible. We talked earlier about your subconscious mind. You're just locking your subconscious mind into your goals and where you want to go and who you want to be and how you want to show up. It's really powerful.
turns.zh: 我从这些录音带中学到了这一点。上大学时，我有一本绿色笔记本。我当时想加入划船队，可我之前从未划过船。每天早上，我都会在页面顶部写下“我是全美头号划船手”。其实我根本不是——我只是个大一新生，来自中西部，体重135磅，从未接触过船只。但我还是这样写了。然后，我会写下当天要做三件事来朝着这个目标前进。在大学期间，我每天都这样做。结果令人惊叹。我们之前谈到过潜意识。你就是在把潜意识锁定在你的目标、你想成为的人以及你想展现的状态上。这真的很强大。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And that's advice anybody can implement. "I want to be the best [inaudible 00:41:51] founder"-
turns.zh: 这是任何人都能实践的建议。“我想成为最棒的[00:41:51听不清]创始人”——

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: You could do that. You could do that [inaudible 00:41:50] exactly.
turns.zh: 你完全可以做到。你完全可以做到[00:41:50听不清]。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. It's such a simple thing. "I want to be the best product manager. Here's three things I'm doing today to help me along the lines."
turns.zh: 是啊。这其实很简单。“我想成为最出色的产品经理。以下是我今天要做的三件事来助我达成目标。”

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Absolutely. My students have to do this twice a week. It's one of their assignments, and they actually have to turn it in. And I have so many students that say five years later, "I still do this a couple times a week, and it's been unbelievable." I'd say this to all your listeners: you will get more done writing down your goal and three things you're going to do to move toward that goal, you'll get more things done in three months than you will in three years without that.
turns.zh: 绝对没错。我的学生每周必须这样做两次。这是他们的作业之一，而且他们还必须提交报告。很多学生五年后都说：“我至今每周还会这样做几次，效果惊人。”我想对所有听众说：写下你的目标和三项行动计划，你能在三个月内完成更多任务，比三年不做要强得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome thing to just try tomorrow at work. Write this down, see how it goes. The coach point, I just want to highlight that. What convinced me to get a coach back when I was working is I just realized, one, every athlete has a coach that tells them, "Here's how to become better," slash, everyone that you work with that is a leader and exec basically has a coach. And the people that have an exec coach will do better in their career and life than those who don't. So why would you not have someone there just helping you become better at this craft? It just makes so much sense if you can afford it. There are different price points for different coaches. Most people can probably afford it in some [inaudible 00:43:09].
turns.zh: 这在明天工作中就能尝试。写下目标，看看效果如何。我想强调教练的观点。我决定请教练的关键原因是，我意识到，每个运动员都有教练告诉他们“如何变得更出色”，每个领导者和高管也都有教练。而拥有高管教练的人，在事业和生活中会比没有的人表现得更好。那么，为什么不找人帮助你提升这项技能呢？如果你负担得起，这太有意义了。不同教练的价格不尽相同，大多数人都能负担得起。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: That's right. That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sweet. Okay. Let's talk about another framework that you have that you call nine lives. And this is essentially another way, it's like another way to hack your brain to come up with things you really should be doing, probably. Talk about this exercise.
turns.zh: 不错。好的，让我们再聊聊你提到的另一个框架，叫做“九种人生”。本质上，这是一种另类的方式，可以通过激发大脑潜能，帮助你找到真正该去做的事。来讲讲这个练习吧。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: So this idea of what's my passion and what's my career goal, it can be really intimidating. And it is intimidating. And so this exercise is to make it less intimidating. And you basically come up with nine lives. So you say your first life, life one is the life you have now. So when I did this exercise ... let's pretend I did this exercise when I'm right out of school, taking that job. So life one is I'm working at this big firm, I live in the Bay Area, here's what I'm doing. That's life one. (00:44:05): There's two rules. The first rule is all the lives have to start from today. So you can't go back in time. They all start from today. And the second rule is you have to be excited about all these lives. So I might say, "Hey, my second life is I want to start a private equity firm and be a founder and be a CEO." And that's life too. And life three is I want to be an author and I want to write whatever fiction or nonfiction. And then life four would be I want to be a professor and teach. And life five is maybe I want to make videos and be on social media. And life six, I want to be an actor. And you go through this whole list of these lives. (00:44:43): And the idea is that ... A couple of things from this exercise. One is let's say that you're in a position where you need to be working in the job you're in. There might be one of these lives that gives you the most energy, and it's the thing if you knew you wouldn't fail, you would do this one. And it's good to recognize what that is and then pull that life a little bit into your current life. (00:45:10): So let's say, Lenny, that you were a product manager, but you really loved doing podcasts, and that was one of your nine lives. Do a podcast every other week, and just pull it into your life, which it sounds like what you did. You started doing it as a side hustle. And then that'll have two amazing effects. One is you will just have more energy everywhere else in your life. Forget if you ever do this full time or not; just the act of pulling something into your life you're really excited about will give you a tremendous amount of energy. (00:45:45): And then the second thing is you'll ideally find the path that is the thing that gives you the most energy. The other thing that I've learned in doing this exercise is you actually can have pretty much all nine lives. You can't have them at once, but if you're fortunate enough to live long enough, you can have all of these things. So I have had the corporate job, been the founder, been the professor, been a writer, had videos, taught people. I've been able to bring most of those lives into this current life.
turns.zh: 关于我的热情所在和职业目标，这个话题确实很让人头疼。确实如此。所以这个练习就是为了让它不那么令人却步。首先你要构想九种人生。第一种人生就是你现在的生活。比如我刚毕业的时候做那份工作，九种人生中的第一种就是在大公司工作，住在湾区，过着现在的生活。（00:44:05）这里有两条规则。第一条是所有人生都要从今天开始，不能回头到过去。第二条是所有人生都要让你感到兴奋。比如我可能会说：“我的第二种人生是创办一家私募股权公司，成为创始人兼CEO。”这也是一种人生。第三种是想成为作家，写小说或非虚构作品。第四种是想成为教授，教书。第五种可能是制作视频，活跃在社交媒体上。第六种是想成为演员。把这整个列表都过一遍。（00:44:43）这个练习的意义在于……有几点启发。比如你现在必须做着当前的工作，但其中某种人生能给你最多能量。如果你知道自己不会失败，就会选择这条路。要认清这条路，然后把它引入到现实生活中。（00:45:10）比如，莱尼，你现在是产品经理，但你真的热爱做播客，而这是你的九种人生之一。你每隔一周做一次播客，这听起来就像你做过的。你把它当作副业开始做。这样会有两个惊人的效果。一是生活中的其他方面都会更有活力。先不说你是否会全职做这件事；只要把你真正热爱的事引入生活，就会给你巨大的能量。（00:45:45）第二点，你最终会找到能给你最多能量的那条路。通过这个练习，我还发现你几乎可以拥有所有九种人生。一次性拥有全部不太现实，但如果你足够幸运、活得足够久，就能体验所有这些生活。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a couple things there that come up as you talk about. One is, on that point, what I do now is my fourth career. First I was an engineer, then I became a founder, then I was a PM, and now I do whatever the heck this is. And I think people don't realize that's how life often goes. You think you're going to do one thing, and then you have many different careers that pivot into [inaudible 00:46:46].
turns.zh: 你提到过程中有几个要点。首先，关于这一点，我现在做的事是我的第四份职业。最初我是工程师，后来成为创始人，再后来做产品经理，现在做着现在这份工作。很多人没意识到生活往往是这样发展的。你以为自己会一直做一件事，但后来会转向许多不同的职业，转向[00:46:46，听不清]。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Exactly. And I think that's the thing. It's just trying to make it a little less intimidating. You don't have to have this one life purpose, passion, thing that you do for the rest of your life. If you just follow the thing that gives you energy at each time, it'll probably be a good indication of where you want to be going.
turns.zh: 确实如此。我觉得关键在于，就是要让这一切不那么令人生畏。你不必非得有一个终身不变的人生目标、激情或事业。如果你只是顺着当下能给你能量的事物前行，这很可能就是你想去的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other thread there is, I know one of your other really important pieces of advice is to avoid this not now idea, where everyone's like, "Here's the thing I should be doing, my genie goal, but not now." Thoughts on just how to think about that, of just like, "Okay, I know I have these lives I could live, but not now," on this or that?
turns.zh: 另外，我知道你另一个很重要的建议是避免那种“现在还不是时候”的想法。每个人都会说：“这是我应该做的事，是我的理想目标，但现在还不是时候。” 你对此有什么看法？比如，“好吧，我知道我可以过上这些生活，但现在还不是时候。”

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, in 20 years of teaching, I've never had a student come to me and say, "Hey, Graham, my real dream is to do X, but I'm just going to give up on it. I'm not going to do it." No one's ever said that. Instead, they say, "Not now." And not now, if they're not careful, will turn into not ever, because not now is just really another way of saying, "I'm not going to do it." And then there's a million reasons why you can't do it now. And those reasons, some of them are legit and some of them are just fear in another form. (00:47:58): In terms of how to overcome that, I think it's kind of hopeful to realize that it's never really the right time. When you're making a change or you're going to go do something different, it's never going to feel secure and safe. You're always going to have some fear. You're always going to feel like you're not ready. You're going to feel like it's too soon. You're going to feel like you don't know exactly what that path looks like. And so just understanding that's normal. That's called entrepreneurship. That's called life. And if you wait for the clouds to part and this ray of sun to come down and say, "Now is the time," you're going to wait your whole life. (00:48:43): And so I think that realization can maybe be helpful. And then try to figure out, what are the things that need to be true for you to launch? And usually for my students, it's something financial that is the big bottleneck. And what I tell them is, "You know what? People have raised money to start a business before. That's happened, where you've had people who've started businesses without their own money that have been able to pay themselves. And that's not a reason to not do it. It's an obstacle. It's something you have to solve, but it's not not an insurmountable obstacle."
turns.zh: 是啊，我教书20年了，从没遇到过学生跟我说：“嘿，格雷厄姆，我真正想做的是X，但我要放弃了。” 从没有人这么说过。他们只会说：“现在还不是时候。” 如果不小心，这“现在还不是时候”就会演变成“永远都不会是时候”，因为“现在还不是时候”其实就是在说“我不会去做这件事”。然后就会找出一堆现在做不了的理由。有些理由是合理的，有些则不过是另一种形式的恐惧。（00:47:58）：说到如何克服这种心理，我觉得意识到“永远没有真正合适的时机”这一点很有希望。当你要做出改变或尝试新事物时，永远不会感到安稳和安全。你总会心怀恐惧，总会觉得自己没准备好，总会觉得时机尚未成熟，总会觉得不清楚未来的道路该怎么走。所以要明白这很正常。这就是创业精神，这就是生活。如果你等着乌云散开，等着那束阳光照下来，然后说：“现在就是时候了，” 那你会等一辈子的。（00:48:43）：所以我觉得这种意识可能会有帮助。然后要思考，要启动这个项目，你需要满足哪些条件？对我的学生来说，财务问题通常是最大的瓶颈。我会告诉他们：“你知道吗？以前也有人靠众筹创业成功过。有人在没有自有资金的情况下创业，最后还能养活自己。这不是不做的理由，而是需要克服的障碍。但这不是不可逾越的障碍。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This touches on a quote I definitely wanted to get to, something that you wrote not long ago. Here's the quote: "The most important thing I've learned in the first 50 years of my life is that the true game of life is an internal one, not an external one. And that journey starts with three powerful words: I am enough." Talk about that. Why is that so important?
turns.zh: 这让我想起你不久前写的一段话，我特别想引用一下。原文是：“我人生前50年学到的最重要的一课是，生命真正的游戏是内在的，而非外在的。这段旅程始于三个强有力的字：我足够好了。” 能谈谈这个吗？为什么这如此重要？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Well, I mean, that's a really a deep topic, but I'll talk about the internal and external journey. So life presents itself as a series of external obstacles and events. And it feels very much like an external journey. And it can feel that way your whole life. But I think what you'll realize, and I started realizing this when I really started meditating and spending time distancing myself from the subconscious thoughts, is a very, very large part of life is internal. I say a very large part because obviously you need some food, clothing, shelter, some basic needs that are external. But for most people that have the ability to even listen to this podcast, I would say the vast majority of your life is internal. (00:50:52): So what do I mean by that? I mean that you're writing a story about what it is you think you need to be happy, or you're writing a story about things you think you need to be to be enough or to be respected or to feel worthy or to get admiration of other people. You're writing that story, and it's just a story. And if you really follow this logic, you'll realize that. You'll realize it is 100% just a story, or it's a story that you should even care. And then that opens up a lot more agency that you have over deciding what is important to you, what is your internal scorecard, what are the things that matter to you, not what the external world thinks or the story you've been writing for a long time. When you start to open this up, it's really kind of scary at first, because you'll start to realize most of the things you're operating from are really just stories that have been written at some point in your life. And so it's actually terrifying at first, and then it starts to become really liberating.
turns.zh: 嗯，我是说，这确实是个深奥的话题，但我还是想谈谈内在与外在的旅程。生活呈现出一系列外在的障碍和事件，感觉这就像一场外在的征程，而且这种感觉可能伴随你一生。但我认为你会意识到——当我真正开始冥想、花时间远离潜意识的思绪时，我开始意识到——生活中的绝大部分都是内在的。我说绝大部分，是因为显然你需要食物、衣物、住所等外在必需品。但对于大多数有能力收听这个播客的人来说，我认为你们生活的绝大部分都是内在的。（00:50:52）那么我这话什么意思呢？我的意思是，你正在编写一个故事，关于你认为自己需要什么才能快乐，或者你认为自己需要成为什么样的人才能被认可、被尊重、感到有价值、获得他人的赞赏。你在编写这个故事，而这不过是个故事。如果你真的遵循这个逻辑，你会意识到这一点。你会意识到这完全就是个故事，或者说这只是个你本不必在意的故事。然后你就能获得更多自主权，去决定什么对你重要，什么是你的内在评分标准，什么才是真正对你重要的，而不是外界的看法或者你长久以来编写的故事。当你开始意识到这一点时，起初可能会感到恐惧，因为你会意识到自己大部分的行为模式都不过是生命中某个时刻编写的故事。起初这确实很可怕，但随后就会变得非常解放人心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Was there an example of that in your life? Because externally, it feels like you're killing it: a killer PE fund, teaching at Stanford. The scorecard is looking good. So it's interesting you say that.
turns.zh: 你生活中有这样的例子吗？因为从外在来看，你似乎做得很成功：管理着一个出色的私募基金，在斯坦福大学任教。你的“评分卡”看起来很亮眼。所以你这么说很有意思。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: The first time I really realized this, it was in 2015. I mentioned to you it took me 14 years to be successful. So we had just sold the last company from our second fund, which is where we really got paid. I had a financial event that was ... it wasn't like I never have to work again in my life. It was just like I could exhale a little bit. I knew I was going to be able to pay my mortgage and put my kids through college. It was that kind of an event. And for a couple days I was euphoric, because I felt like I'd worked so hard for this. I'd been, again, at this for 15 years, but really longer than that, if you go back to getting into college. And the whole thing had been a long journey. (00:53:05): And then it hit me that nothing changed. Nothing internally changed at all. I still had the same problems. I still felt the same way about myself. I still had a lot of negative thoughts about myself. This goal that I thought that I had for this whole long period of time, it didn't actually change anything. It changed externally, for sure. Like I said, I could exhale and pay my mortgage. And those are all really good things. But that was the first time when I realized, "Oh, wait a second. It's really up to me to find things that are going to give me joy. And the achievement of some kind of external event is not one of those things." (00:53:54): And I know that sounds really, really weird, but there's so many people that I've heard that have had very, very similar stories. And so it was really disorienting for me. And actually it was the first time in my life where I experienced depression, because I just had this thought of, "I think I was working my whole life for that, and it wasn't what I thought it was going to be." And so now I was thinking, "Well, what is it then? What is the thing that's going to give me joy?" And that takes some introspection to ask those questions.
turns.zh: 我第一次真正意识到这一点是在2015年。我跟你说过，我花了14年才取得成功。当时我们刚刚卖掉了第二支基金中的最后一家公司，这才是我们真正开始赚到钱的时候。我经历了一场财务事件……这并不意味着我余生都不用工作了。只是说我可以稍微松口气了。我知道自己能还清房贷，让孩子们上大学。这就是那种转变。接下来的几天我欣喜若狂，因为我觉得自己为此付出了太多努力。我又为此奋斗了15年，甚至更久——从考上大学算起。这整个过程实在太漫长了。（00:53:05）但随后我意识到，内在的一切并未改变。我仍然面临着同样的问题，对自己的看法依然如故。我对自己仍有很多负面评价。这个我奋斗了这么久的目标，实际上并没有带来任何改变。外在情况当然有所改观。正如我所说，我可以松口气，还清房贷了。这些都是好事。但那是我第一次意识到：“哦，等等。这真的取决于我自己去寻找能给我带来快乐的东西。某个外部事件带来的成就感，并非其中之一。”（00:53:54）我知道这听起来很奇怪，但我听过太多人有着非常相似的经历。这对我来说真的很令人迷茫。事实上，那是我人生中第一次经历抑郁，因为我只是在想：“我以为我为此奋斗了一辈子，可结果却并非我所期望的。” 所以现在我在想：“那到底是什么？什么才能给我带来快乐？”要找到这些答案，需要进行深刻的自我反思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was just having a conversation with a friend who's an angel investor, and he just had a bunch of exits. And he's like, "Cool, I got some money in my bank account now, but I don't feel anything. I thought I'd be like, 'Holy moly, this is exactly what I was hoping for. And nothing changed.'" Exactly how you're describing.
turns.zh: 我刚和一位天使投资人朋友聊天，结果他刚完成了一系列退出项目。他说：“不错，我银行账户里现在有钱了，但我毫无感觉。我原本以为自己会大喊‘天哪，这正是我所期望的’。结果却毫无变化。” 这和你描述的感受一模一样。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: I think you get a little bit of peace of mind when you have some financial security, which is valuable. But in terms of now my life changes, now I'm enough, now I am happy, now I feel good about myself, none of that changes, for really anybody that I know.
turns.zh: 我觉得当你获得一定的财务保障时，会获得些许心安，这确实很有价值。但就我认识的所有人而言，现在的生活并没有因此发生改变，现在的我依然充实，依然快乐，依然对自己充满信心。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the hardest part, as you said, is you think it will. You think, "Oh, I'll be so happy once I achieve this thing." And I think an example of this is there's a lot of miserable billionaires, from what I've read and see. And that should tell you a lot.
turns.zh: 而最困难的部分，正如你所说，是你以为它会带来改变。你会想：“一旦实现这个目标，我就会无比快乐。” 我认为一个例子就是，我读到和看到过很多亿万富翁过得非常痛苦。这应该能说明很多问题。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Maybe a second-to-last question; I'm curious if there's anything recently you're focused on, have been thinking a lot about that maybe you changed your mind about, or has changed the way you think about the world?
turns.zh: 或许最后一个问题：我很好奇你最近有没有专注于某件事，有没有反复思考过某些问题，或者有没有改变对世界的看法？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: The last two years, I had my two oldest boys go off to college, 2022 and then 2024. And that really hit hard. You would think that I would've been preparing for that for 18 years for each of them, but for some reason it just really hit me really, really hard. And I think it was a real wake up call of mortality, I guess, and to realize that nothing goes on forever. And these wonderful people that I had lived with, each for 18 years, were no longer going to really be a part of my daily life. (00:56:17): And that really set me off on a journey of a lot of spiritual work, doing a lot of meditating and working with some gurus. And it's been really profound. And it's put me a lot closer in touch with the things that really matter to me. I've given myself more permission to spend time doing those things than the normal external world type things. So that was a pretty profound change for me. And the spiritual journey is arguably really the important journey. And this could be a longer conversation. And maybe you have the luxury of doing that journey as you get older or something, but it's been a really profound, profound journey.
turns.zh: 过去两年，我两个最大的儿子先后离家上大学，分别在2022年和2024年。这真的让我深受打击。你可能会觉得，我为每个孩子都准备了18年，但不知为何，这份打击实在太强烈了。我想这让我深刻意识到生命无常，意识到与我共同生活了18年的这些美好的人，将不再成为我日常生活的一部分。（00:56:17）这也促使我踏上了深刻的精神探索之旅，进行了大量冥想，并与一些导师合作。这段经历意义非凡，让我更深刻地认识到真正重要的东西。我给了自己更多许可，把时间花在这些事情上，而非追逐外界的浮华事物。这对我来说是一个重大的转变。可以说，精神探索之旅才是最重要的旅程。关于这个话题，我们可以深入探讨。或许等你年纪再大些，就有机会从容地开启这段旅程了，但对我而言，这是一次意义深远的精神觉醒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to see what insights come out of this part of your life. Final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. We have this segment on the podcast called Failure Corner, where people come on this podcast, they share all these wins: "Oh, I have this amazing PE fund that's killing it. I teach at Stanford. I've launched all these things. All these students, they're so great. Life's amazing. Nothing ever goes wrong," when in reality, it does. And those stories often aren't told. So I'm curious if there's a story you could share of a time you failed in your career and, if you learned something from that experience, what you learned.
turns.zh: 我很期待听到你人生中这一阶段的深刻见解。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后一个问题：在我们的播客中，有一个名为“失败角”的环节。通常嘉宾们都会分享成功故事，比如“我的私募基金业绩斐然”、“我在斯坦福任教”、“成功创立了多家公司”、“学生们都特别棒，生活无比美好”等等。但现实中难免会遭遇挫折，而这些故事往往未被讲述。不知你能否分享一段职业生涯中的失败经历，以及从中获得的启示。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yeah, I'll tell a couple stories. So when I was in high school, I wrestled. And I cut a lot of weight to make the varsity team. And I was not in the best mental place because of cutting weight. But anyway, I lost a big match my junior year. And I quit and I never wrestled again. And that haunted me. So first of all, that was a failure, a big failure for me. And it really haunted me. And so I, after that, made a promise to myself that it wasn't going to have that happen again. When I went to college, I tried to row crew. I failed year after year trying to make the team, trying to make the boat. Eventually had some real success my senior year, but prior to that, just failure after failure. (00:58:44): And then at Alpine, I mean, we lost money on our first fund. We had real trouble during the recession. I think five of my first eight investments I ever made in my life, I lost money. And in venture world, that's one thing, but in private equity, that's a whole different ratio, which is not a good ratio at all. When I first started teaching, I wasn't good at teaching, had a lot of insecurities. I was really young when I started, and I didn't feel like I had really anything to share with the students. And I think that showed up, and it took me a long time to kind of figure that out. (00:59:26): So I guess almost my entire track record is one that starts with things not going well, and then just over a long period of time of chipping away, looks like a success on paper. But anytime early in the process would look like an abject failure. So I'm quite familiar with failure in the form of setbacks. I think the ultimate failure though was the wrestling one, where I just quit. That was really the only one I would characterize as a failure. The other ones, because I kept going and staying with it, turned out to work out well, with a lot of scars and bruises, but the failure would've been quitting.
turns.zh: 是啊，我可以讲几个故事。高中时，我参加过摔跤比赛。为了能进入校队，我拼命减重。但由于减重过度，心理状态很不稳定。结果高三那年，我输掉了一场重要比赛。之后我退出了，再也没有继续摔跤。这件事一直困扰着我。所以首先，那次失败对我来说是个重大挫折，深深地折磨着我。因此，我向自己承诺，再也不会让这种情况发生了。上大学后，我尝试过划船运动，但年复一年都未能入选队伍。直到大四那年才取得了一些成绩，但之前都是一连串的失败。（00:58:44）在Alpine公司，我们的首支基金亏损了。经济衰退期间，我们遇到了巨大挑战。我人生前八次投资，有五次都亏损了。在风险投资领域，亏损是常事，但在私募股权领域，这个比例实在太高了。刚开始教书时，我教学水平不佳，充满不安。当时我太年轻，觉得自己没什么能传授给学生的知识。这点显而易见，我花了很长时间才想明白。（00:59:26）所以我觉得我的人生经历几乎都是先经历挫折，然后经过长时间的努力，才在纸面上看起来成功。但在过程初期，这些都像是彻底的失败。所以我对挫折式的失败非常熟悉。不过最严重的失败还是摔跤那次，我直接退出了。那是唯一一次我会定义为彻底失败的经历。其他失败，因为我坚持不懈，最终都得到了好的结果，尽管历经伤痛，但如果当时选择放弃，那才是真正的失败。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that the circles back to your core advice of stick with it. Most things that are important take a long time and there's a lot of suffering [inaudible 01:00:24].
turns.zh: 我很欣赏你最后回归到坚持这个核心建议。大多数重要的事情都需要长期努力，过程中会有很多痛苦[01:00:24不可听清]。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yeah, they do. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊，他们确实如此。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I wanted to ask, I can't help but ask at this point, because I think a lot of people are wondering this, just when do you quit? When should you quit something? Because some things are just not worth it. Is there any advice there you could share?
turns.zh: 我想问个问题，这个时候忍不住要问，因为我觉得很多人都在好奇，你什么时候该放弃？什么时候该退出某件事？因为有些事情根本不值得坚持。你能分享一下这方面的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Yes, for sure. I think the time to quit is when you can no longer see the vision and you can no longer really believe the vision. And then when that happens for a long period of time ... or maybe you're no longer even excited about the vision; somewhere in there, I think. The excited one, you have to be a little careful of, because in the dark days, exciting is not the word you're going to use. But at least in our company, for the first 10 years it was not going well. But each time, we'd make fewer mistakes, we'd start to see something working. We'd do one really good deal in this fund, we'd start to learn from that. We'd get one really good hire, we'd learn from that. We would little by little start to see these green shoots. (01:01:24): And I have this unbelievable statement. I didn't write it. Dan and Chip Heath wrote it in their book, Switch, which is "Scale your bright spots. Find what's working and do more of that." And as you start to progress, for me, for example, at Alpine, almost all the time, we always had at least a small glimmer of a bright spot. And then we'd scale that and then we'd continue forward and we'd find some more and we'd scale those. And over time, all those bright spots became our business. That became what we did. That became our strategy. That became how we hired people. That became where we recruited from. All those bright spots just started to magnify until the entire business was pretty much a bright spot. But it took time, because we had to figure out where those were. And we had to do a lot of things wrong to figure out where the bright spots were.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。我认为放弃的时机是当你再也看不到愿景，再也无法真正相信这个愿景的时候。然后当这种情况持续很长一段时间……或者也许你甚至对这个愿景都不再感兴趣了；我觉得就是在这种情况下。在兴奋感消失的时候，你得多加留心，因为在低谷时期，“兴奋”这个词可不是你会用到的。但至少在我们公司，前十年的发展并不顺利。但每次，我们都会少犯一些错误，开始看到一些成效。我们会在这只基金里做一笔很成功的交易，从中吸取经验。我们会招到一个非常出色的员工，从中总结经验。我们会一点一点地看到这些希望的萌芽。（01:01:24）我有这样一句令人惊叹的话。这句话不是我写的，是丹·希思和奇普·希思在《开创》一书中提到的：“放大你的亮点。找到有效的方法并加以推广。” 对我来说，比如在Alpine公司，几乎每次我们都能看到至少一丝亮光。然后我们会放大这些亮点，再继续前进，找到更多亮点，不断放大。随着时间推移，所有这些亮点最终就构成了我们的业务。这成了我们的核心策略，成了我们招聘的标准，成了我们人才选拔的依据。所有这些亮点逐渐汇聚，最终整个业务几乎都成了亮点。但这需要时间，因为我们必须先找出这些亮点所在。我们必须犯很多错误，才能找到亮点所在之处。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Graham, is there anything else that you wanted to share or you think is important to leave listeners with before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 格雷厄姆，在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想分享的，或者你认为对听众很重要的事情吗？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: I mean, I think what I would say is just in general, you got one life, you get one shot. And so take the time to really figure out and answer the question, what does a wonderful, amazing, incredible life look like? And just get as clear as you possibly can on that. No matter how crazy or aspirational it seems, write it down. Write down that thing is write down that thing that would make this life amazing. And write it down for your life, your career, your relationships, your friends, your body, your spirituality, your financial situation. And just the first magic is just knowing what you want. And I'd say 90% of people never even know what they want. So take the time to do that. And the more clear you are on that, the more invested you are in that, the more likely you are to make it come true.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想我要说的是，总的来说，你只有一次生命，你只有一次机会。所以花时间真正思考并回答这个问题：一个美好、令人惊叹、不可思议的生活是什么样的？尽可能清晰地想清楚这一点。无论这看起来多么疯狂或充满雄心壮志，把它写下来。写下那些能让生活变得美好的东西。写下你生活、事业、人际关系、朋友、身体、精神生活和财务状况中的美好愿景。只要你知道自己想要什么，第一步就成功了。我敢说，90%的人甚至都不知道自己想要什么。所以花时间想清楚这一点吧。你对此越清晰，越投入，就越有可能实现目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I love about that is you don't have to do this thing, just step one is understand what it could be if you could do that.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这一点的是，你不必做什么事，只要第一步是理解如果能做到这一点会是什么样子。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's almost like understand where your Google directions could take you if you turned off autopilot. Oh, man. Okay. Well, with that, Graham, we reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 这几乎就像是了解如果关闭自动驾驶模式，谷歌导航会带你去哪里一样。天哪。好吧，那好，格雷厄姆，我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节了。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Let's do it.
turns.zh: 开始吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，哪两三本书是你最常向别人推荐的？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: So in the realm of a lot of the topics we've been talking about, which is your internal and external game, I love the book Untethered Soul. And I love the book, Don't Believe Everything You Think. They have very similar themes, but they come at it differently. But I think both of those will really change your perspective if you read them. (01:04:08): And then a very, very practical book that's probably the book I've read more than any other book, is How to Win Friends and Influence People, by Dale Carnegie, which was written in like 1930. There's no other book it. There's a reason that people are still recommending it 100 years after it's written. So it's definitely worth checking out.
turns.zh: 嗯，在我们讨论的很多话题中，比如你的内在和外在修养，我很喜欢《不羁之魂》这本书。我也很喜欢《别轻信你所想》这本书。它们主题相似，但处理方式不同。但我认为，如果你读了这两本书，真的会改变你的视角。（01:04:08）：然后有一本非常实用的书，可能是我读过最多的书，那就是戴尔·卡耐基的《如何赢得朋友并影响他人》，这本书写于1930年左右。没有其他书能像它一样经久不衰。即使在它问世100年后，人们仍然在推荐它。所以绝对值得一读。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, that book, I still think about it often, even though I read it 30 years ago at this point. I love that recommendation. And it's like a very old book to read, but you have to get past the fact that it was written a long time ago. Okay, next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 是啊，那本书我现在还经常回想，尽管我读它已经是30年前的事了。我很喜欢这个推荐。它是一本很古老的书，但你得克服它年代久远的障碍。好的，下一个问题。你有没有最近特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: I, for the first time, watched the movie Where the Crawdads Sing. And I just loved it. It's kind of a romantic comedy, or not comedy, sorry, romantic love story meets murder mystery, meets coming of age. And it really, really touched me. Then I promptly read the book as well, so I love that.
turns.zh: 我第一次看《蝲蛄吟唱的地方》这部电影。我特别喜欢它。这算是一部浪漫喜剧，或者说，不算喜剧，应该是一部爱情悬疑片，夹杂着成长故事。它真的深深打动了我。然后我马上就读了原著，所以我很喜欢这部作品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 你有没有最近发现的特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: I'm a really big fan of sleep. I think it makes a massive difference in your life. And that's a whole other topic we could go down another time. So I have a few things that have helped me on that. So if you saw me sleeping, I have earplugs, I have a noise machine. I have a sleep mask, and then I have a Chilipad that goes on my bed to keep the bed cool. And I sleep great. All those things really help. The earplugs and mask and noise machine allow you to not hear the ambient noise. And then there's a lot of research actually on the temperature at which you want to sleep. And your body goes up and down throughout the night. So this Chilipad that goes under your mattress, there's a whole bunch of versions of that. And that helps a lot.
turns.zh: 我特别注重睡眠。我觉得睡眠对生活影响巨大。这个话题我们可以另找时间深入探讨。所以我有几个帮助睡眠的工具。假如你看到我睡觉，我戴着耳塞，用着噪音机，还有睡眠眼罩。还有床上用的Chilipad降温垫。这些东西真的很有用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I also sleep with an eye mask. My wife and I rotate the earplugs, because someone has to pay attention to the baby, in case he wakes up.
turns.zh: 我还戴着睡眠眼罩。我和妻子轮流使用耳塞，因为总得有人留意宝宝，免得他醒来。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: There you go. Yeah.
turns.zh: 好的，就是这样。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this Chilipad, is this the Eight Sleep, or is this in just a cold bag?
turns.zh: 这个Chilipad，是Eight Sleep的吗？还是只是冷敷袋？

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: Well, no. So I actually bought the Eight Sleep, and it was too much.
turns.zh: 不是的。我买了Eight Sleep，但太复杂了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's a lot.
turns.zh: 是啊，它功能太多了。

turns.speaker: Graham Weaver
turns.en: It would turn on and off. And I would wake up. And then it would track my sleep, and then I'd start to freak out because it'd tell me I wasn't sleeping well. So I actually returned it and I got a really simple one called OOLER. And it just turns on and off. There's no timing. There's no any weird functionality. And it was a lot cheaper, and it works better for me. So everyone use their own thing, but that one worked better for me.
turns.zh: 它会自动开关。我就会醒来。然后它会记录睡眠情况，结果显示我睡眠不好，然后我就开始焦虑。所以我退货了，买了一个很简单的，叫OOLER。它就是开关，没有定时功能，也没有其他复杂设置。便宜得多，而且对我更有效。所以大家可以根据自己的情况选择，但这个对我更合适。

turns.en: Really happy to talk about that about. So I'll answer the question more like, what's a little bit of a different philosophy that we have? So when we were coming out of the recession and I hired this coach, we looked at all of our companies. And we were looking for where did we make our most money, and what was the most consistent trend? And we looked at valuation, growth rates, capital structure, geography, industry. We cut the data every way you could imagine. And we had these three companies that kept showing up on all these lists that were three of our top performers, but they didn't seem to really have anything in common. (01:08:53): And then we're like, "Well, they have one thing in common, which is they started off really badly, so badly in fact that we put our own person from Alpine in to go run the company, and then they ended up becoming our best companies." So we said, "Wait a second. Maybe that's the highly correlated thing, is us putting our own team in place, and even upstream of that, maybe just having an incredible management team." So that was foundational. And now, we put our own leadership team in 100% of the time. And not only that, but we have spent an inordinate amount of time trying to build a program to help people who are in their late 20s, early 30s learn how to become CEOs. And that's been foundational. (01:09:38): So the thing that we probably believe to be true that not that many people agree with us on is that the management team is really where we think all the alpha comes from. You can't get the industry wrong, because if you hire the best management team in the world to run a typewriter business, you're going to lose money. So you can't be wrong on the industry, but you also don't have to be perfect on the industry. You have to have a good enough industry and then a world-class management team. And we found that to be a really good formula for consistent returns. And it's way more fun because you're literally in a board meeting with someone that is on your side of the table, because you hired them and put them in. And so you're building the company together. And they're bringing a lot of similar values. And so it's been a real differentiator for us.
turns.zh: 很乐意谈谈我们的不同理念。在经济衰退后复苏期间，我聘请了一位教练，我们审视了所有投资组合公司。我们研究哪家公司赚得最多，最稳定的趋势是什么？我们从估值、增长率、资本结构、地域、行业等各个维度切入数据。但最后三家公司始终在各类榜单上脱颖而出，它们都是我们的顶级表现者，但它们似乎并没有太多共同点。（01:08:53）：然后我们发现，它们唯一的共同点是起步阶段表现糟糕——糟糕到我们不得不派Alpine内部人员去接管公司，最终这些公司却成了我们最成功的案例。所以我们意识到，关键在于我们派遣自己的团队上阵，甚至更上游的环节，关键在于拥有卓越的管理团队。这是基础要素。如今，我们百分百采用这种模式。不仅如此，我们还投入大量精力打造一个项目，帮助20多岁、30出头的人学习如何成为CEO。这也是关键要素。（01:09:38）：我们坚信，管理团队才是创造超额收益的核心。你不可能选错行业，因为即便你聘请全球顶尖管理团队去运营一家打字机公司，也注定亏损。所以行业选择不能出错，但也不必完美。只要行业尚可，拥有世界级管理团队就足够了。我们发现，这正是实现稳定回报的黄金配方。更重要的是，这种模式带来了更深层次的乐趣——因为你在董事会会议上面对的是与你立场一致的人，因为是你亲自聘请并培养了他们。如此一来，我们共同打造公司，他们也秉持着相似的价值观。这正是我们的核心竞争力所在。
